sp: JESSICA WALKER President and CEO, Manhattan Chamber of Commerce
p:
Good afternoon. My name is Jean-Homer Lautrice. I do have a written statement that I’d like to submit. Okay, my name is Jean-Homer Lautrice. I’m an organizer with Unite Here Local 100. We represent tons of thousands of hospitality workers in New York City and the surrounding region. Our diverse members span many of the iconic sites New Yorkers know and love, large stadiums where staff create new experiences for all who attend. Our members will be the people who will be on the ground when the global communities arrive for the FIFA 2026 World Cup in New York.

Our members want this tournament to go well for visitors and leave thinking New York delivered something special. What we’re asking for isn’t complicated nor difficult. Our concerns boil down to this, if a contractor is doing World Cup related work, there needs to be enforceable labor standards attached to that contract. Existing collective bargaining agreements must be honored. Workers who want to organize shouldn’t face interference and subcontracting chains need to be transparent so that there’s no question about who employs them and who is responsible when something goes wrong. What we’re saying and asking for can’t be aspirational statements buried in a press release. The things we’re concerned with are critical for the wellbeing of our members. That families have sustainable jobs. They need to be binding, legally enforceable with real oversight behind them. We would be doing a disservice to our members through this process in the City of New York if we didn’t say plainly that we see what we’ve seen happen before.

Multinational events generally have a low road track record. Large groups will say the right thing to secure RFP and then leave the communities that made big promises behind. In the element of that is low road subcontracting, a practice where wage structures that don’t come close to matching the scale of the event along with health and safety conditions nobody would expect if cameras were pointed at them. New York should not be the next city where this happens. A World class event requires wage and hour standards commiserate with global excellence. These aren’t abstract concerns. The people we represent will staff the stadiums. Our members will prepare their food, run the concessions, clean the facilities. They will be the first face a visitor sees and the last person to leave when the night is over. The work our members perform because they are also on stage, takes skill, training, and deserves stability. Treating these jobs as interchangeable or temporary bodies to fill schedules during the busy week is not acceptable. Beyond that, it is not consistent with what the CD says it stands for. New

York has an opportunity here to not just host a successful tournament but demonstrate a city can do this right. With that you can run a mega event without running over the people who make it happen and who make it work. This is not abstract. Just last week, FIFA cancelled their firm festival in Liberty State Park, sacrificing thousands of hours for hardworking union members and undermining the wage floor for the writ large - for the event with large. Unite Here Local 100 is prepared to be a proactive partner but partnership is predicated up on our members interest in the room, on paper and demoralizing a contract. Thank you.

Good afternoon Madam Chair Congratulations on your first hearing members of the Committee. I’m Jeff LeFrancois, Executive Director of the Meat Packing District Management Association and today, I’m also here as Co-Chair of the New York City BID Association, which is the member organization for the city’s 78 business improvement districts with representation across the five boroughs for Meat Packing to Montague street and up to Morris Park, Flatbush to Flatiron and in Chinatown

and now at the beach at Coney Island. BIDs are a direct reflection of their communities and collectively invest over $200 million in private assessment funds in their communities each year. BIDs are not just neighborhood managers. We are proven partners in bringing public spaces to life. Our programs help to find the city’s cultural calendar from the ball drop to sprawling art installations, holiday lights, and organized tastes of our districts. We make it happen. Every day BIDs of all sizes are partners with the city in providing supplemental city services to keep our commercial corridors clean, safe, beautiful and indeed bustling, while also working to bring world class programming to our neighborhoods. BIDs want to do big things. We were referenced many times today and as managers of the public realm, we are required to apply for permits through the street activities permit office. However, there is currently a moratorium on Plaza activations from June 1, to July 18th because of the World Cup. This moratorium is preventing us from being able to move forward with any programming whatsoever, including things like lunchtime concerts

and free workout classes, soccer centric programming aside. While City Hall has indicated that they are working to find a solution and that SAPA will be reformed, planning takes time for organizations no matter their size, so guidance on how BIDs can participate and apply for permits cannot come soon enough. As we also prepare to welcome millions of visitors, we know our hotel supply will not meet demand. The city’s expensive onerous special permit process has all but halted the development of new hotels while simultaneously undermining membership growth for our unions. Our ever more expensive hotel rates are eliminating huge swaths of travelers from picking NYC as their preferred destination for the Cup. And while that change won’t happen overnight, it's something the Council should seriously consider. Public transit must also be prioritized. Nobody wants to miss a goal because of a double parked car in a bus lane or because of a delayed train. We really look forward to working with this Committee. I really appreciate the opportunity today and of course with City Hall to ensure success across every

corner of this city and then no matter the team we support, there’s a great program at which you can experience the best of

Thank you so much. We’ll jump into questions starting with the first set of speakers from HTC. Some economists have cautioned that hotel prices could displace traditional tourists. Is that something that HTC is also concerned about?
So it’s about demand this summer.
And displacing traditional summer tourists.
Placing traditional summer tourists. It’s an interesting question. I would have to study it more and get back to you.
We can expect a large influx of people and my question is around hotel workers and what you expect in terms of workload, scheduling, staffing levels to shift during the World Cup period.

Yeah, that’s a great question. Yeah, we recently did a survey of our membership and we found that 40 percent of our

members don’t have enough say to cover a $400 emergency expense. About half are spending more than half of their monthly income on housing and about one-third have fallen behind on rents or mortgage payments in the last year. So, our members, despite our great contract, are struggling with affordability like other New Yorkers and also struggling with work loads. Work intensity in the hotel industry has gone up in the post pandemic era as hotels are experimenting in various ways to computerize and automate and increase the workload. And yeah, we expect a busy summer and hope to be able to meet the influx in tourist demands with a fair contract and a professional workforce.
Can you add more details of what hotel workers are fighting for in the new contract?

Yeah uhm, it’s a great question. We’re fighting for a number of measures to make New York more affordable for our members. We’re fighting to protect our family healthcare plan to protect and improve our pension. To have wages that have caught up with the rising cost of living and to win some of the things we’ve won in New Jersey

including, you know, a childcare fund and other measures to make the work more sustainable and so that our workers can afford to live in the city that they work.
And what is the risk? I know the contract is expiring July 1st. What is the risk that the World Cup operations could be impacted?

Yeah, it’s a great question. You know our members are professional. They love the work that they do and they want to keep doing it, especially during such a you know a high profile events. Everyone is excited to be a part of it and so, the hope is that the industry comes to the table and uhm, you know agrees to terms that help our members do that. Help them serve the influx of tourists that they would love to meet and to welcome to our city.

Council Member Gutiérrez. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much Chair. Thank you for your testimony. I have two questions. One is for you, you mentioned that you - what is your profession at one of the hotels, my apologies.

Housekeeping.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Housekeeping. Do you have - do you have any concerns or have expressed any interest in additional training? Obviously we’re anticipating an influx of people from all over but as a housekeeper, do you have any concern just for your own personal safety, considering the magnitude of people that will be coming in and out potentially for your personal safety or has your hotel instituted any additional training for you all? You know my mother was a housekeeper. My mother in law was a hotel housekeeper, retired from the union, so all my respect goes to you all and oftentimes, you all are the frontlines, right? And so, what are some of the concerns that you and other housekeepers have for you know this magnitude of potential guests that you’ll be having. Are there tools that you all have to be able to identify certain issues and I don’t mean to put any pressure on you. I know you guys are expected to do the job and identify other, you know trafficking potentially. What are some of those tools that you have and/or are you expecting to get that training? And then the next question is for you. Sorry, thank you.

I would say our safety or housekeeping safety of the hotel. That’s my concern. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: That’s your main concern and has there been a response from the hotel or is there an expectation of additional training or what other safety precautions would you like to see to be able to protect you all?
We have training about trafficking, human trafficking. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, you’ve already done the training? Are they doing more training or?

I don’t know. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: No, okay, alright. Well something I continue to raise with folks. And then and I apologize, the gentleman from Unite Here. Thank you so much for your testimony. Uhm, my question is, your testimony is great. I think it really captures the fact that there’s a - or maybe an event that’s temporary. There is a much longer standing impact and I know you mentioned in your testimony about the festival that was cancelled last minute. Uhm, what is - what do you think the leverage that we have is for some of these like permanent jobs

that you’re speaking about and how will you all - are you able to bring on more people at this point? Like what is the best thing to do for workers and like the economically responsible thing to do to prepare. And I’m sorry if it’s a loaded question but I’m genuinely curious because I think we all see this and go like, oh this means jobs but it doesn’t always mean jobs. It may not always mean jobs beyond the event. So, kind of how have you thought that through and what are some of the things that like we can help in asking for and leveraging? Thank you Chair.

Very loaded but awesome question. Well, I think we have the past to look back to learn from. We’ve had even it’s like this, not in New York but in other parts of our country where the investment became long term where we saw benefits going beyond that calendar where the city and the state and so on benefitted in very long term greatly from you know not just tourists coming into visit but where there’s sustainable visits and return visits and industries that can actually not just born in services but also that can grow from it. So, I think we need to look at not just labor but the City of New York and partners, how do we benefit? How do

we capitalize on the opportunities that are coming but from labor, we have to look at how do we make these jobs sustainable? How do we make sure that our members, whether it’s HTC, Unite Here Local 100, and other unions in other trades, how do we make sure that our members are benefitting? Not just in this contract but long term and what part of the growth of New York City because New York City is going to be greatly benefitting from this opportunity and we’re going to grow from it but we’re interested in all of us going together. I think that’s New York's - that’s one of the things that makes New York great, right. When we are all growing together, we become even a greater and a better city, not that that’s the interest is how do we look beyond this event which is awesome and once in a lifetime. Uhm, but what are the industries that are going to benefit long term, serve as an industry that may even be born out of this event and how do we work together to make sure that labor is not forgotten and left behind? COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Absolutely, I mean it’s almost March, so we got to work together quickly to brainstorm but uhm, thank you all so much for your testimony. Thank you Chair.
Thank you.
Everyone feels the urgency. Uhm, I wanted to speak a bit about the BIDs. What engagement have you had to date with the Administration? Or have BIDs-

Sure, there’s been some large scale, the webinar is a reference, sort of like putting out the information that the city appears to have thus far. You know this restriction on our ability to get permits. It seems to be a deference to FIFA and their desire of what they do and do not want to do across the city and like I said, that’s not just preventing us from planning World Cup specific activations but the lunch time stuff, the free workout classes. All the other things that we do in that prime two month timeframe. So, we’ve been told that the Administration is keen to get us information on how we can begin to apply for permits and there have been a number of meetings like I said, mostly large scale as it relates to sort of them putting out information. Uhm, Council Member Gutiérrez just said it’s March, that is very true and it makes me very nervous given this is you know happening in June. So, we are

eager to be at the table getting real information on how we can make this stuff happen.
And typically when you’re planning for summer events, how much lead time do you usually have?

The city mandates depending on the size of the event. If it’s a neighborhood activation, they want at least for the permit to be in the system at least two months prior to but sometimes for us, like if we know we have a big event coming, we’re putting that in six months in advance right and then, coordination across numerous agencies to make these things happen. So, right now it’s that you know some of us have big, big teams that can do this stuff. Some BIDs are a staff of one or two people making these things happen. So, it’s the coordination internally and then how and whether or not the city and its agencies will be able to meet the demand of what we hope is you know activations across all five boroughs.
So, you mentioned a multiweek moratorium on events?
Yes, right now, we cannot put permits in the system for June 1 to July 18th at all for anything.
And what is the rationale you’ve been told on that?

Our understanding is that went into effect in the previous Administration and that uhm that was to give the city the ability to have FIFA uhm choose where they would like to activate. I think for the record, I don’t think this is unreasonable. What's unreasonable is that it’s March and we don’t have an indication of what FIFA even wants to do across the five boroughs. So, that is our sort of eagerness and the desire to you know let’s - we want to make big things happen I think as you in all your opening remarks acknowledged. There's a huge benefit to gain from this.

Certainly understand the urgency and the need for more clarity here. Beyond clarity on the permits, what other resources or information do you need from the city to create the great programming that we all know and love.

Absolutely, I mentioned the private resources that BIDs invest in their

communities but again, you know we heard a lot about the public dollars that are being spent on this. How will those be allocated across not just BID districts but community organizations as well, right? You know, I have colleagues whose annual budget is less than half a million dollars. What is that organization going to do as it relates to a program in their community? Is the city going to be willing to bring money to that community or not based on everything they’ve laid out. You know if we’re going to talk about equity, how will that be looked at across all five boroughs, I think is really important as well. I think many of us who have the ability, understanding of events, want just the ability to do just that and then be permitted and allowed to do so and plan accordingly. So, really considering the full gamut of what we can offer and how the city can get behind it is what’s most important.
Thank you so much.
Absolutely, thank you.

Any further questions? Alright, thank you so much for your testimony, really informative and I appreciate you being here. Next,

we have Tarek Pertew from Footy, uhm, Minky Worden from Human Rights Watch, uhm, Gonzalo Casals from Culture and Arts Policy Institute, and Michele Dottin from Independent Drivers Guild. Thank you very much for being here and we can begin testimony, whoever would like to start. Go ahead, yeah. Thank you, yeah -
Two minutes each.

I’m going to rush through it. Thank you Madam Chair. Congratulations on your first hearing. My name is Gonzalo Casals. I’m the Co-Director of the Culture and Arts Policy Institute. I’m also - was the former, I’m former Commissioner for the Department of Cultural Affairs during the last Administration. The New York City Comptroller's Office established that the creative sector generates $110 billion annually, 13 percent of the city’s total economic output and we employ over 326,000 people paying out $30 billion in wages. New York City hosts an astonishing 12 percent of all those U.S. clear industry jobs, despite accounting only for less than three percent of total national employment.

All this to say that you know we’re a big industry in New York City and [INAUDIBLE 119:04] on this May, the cultural organizations, all these cultural workers have not been mentioned at all in this hearing as potential partners for this work. The question before this Committee is whether the city will leverage this global tournament on our local culturing sector to drive core economic development or leave money on the table by training culture as merely peripheral to programming. The World Cup is projected to generate a massive $3.3 billion in economic activity for New York and New Jersey and over $1.2 million BCR’s and generate $431 million in state and local tax revenues. To maximize this, we recommend that the city use the World Cup as a coordinator, cultural catalyst, especially the city should partner with civil society, cultural organizations to be specific, to extend FIFA 2026 BM stadiums into citywide cultural celebration rooted in neighborhoods across all five boroughs. Throughout the tournament, New Yorkers and visitors should experience hundreds of free concerts, events in parks and plazas, open street libraries,

cultural institutions and beads of course. This approach will generate an immediate neighborhood level economic impact by capturing visitor foot traffic across all five boroughs, supporting small businesses and strengthening the hospitality sector. To understand this potential, consider the local multiplier effect. A study of New York City theaters found that the economic multipliers 2.2. That means for every dollar that we generate by a local cultural venue, 1.20 cents circulates in surrounding neighborhood businesses. A return significantly higher than the 1.65 multiplier city median entertainment. Crucially, the city would also create paid opportunities for artists and cultural workers. The tournament is expected to support over 26,000 jobs and generate $1.3 million in labor income. We must ensure that this wealth is distributed equitably to workers across the city. Implementation through a city led public private partnership with much in funds and defined roles for [INAUDIBLE 121:15]. One designated organization per portal will provide fiscal sponsorship, coordination

and set sublets to local partners to ensure coherence and equitable distribution. Centralized branding and streamlined permitting would [INAUDIBLE 121:31]. Would ensure local relevance and accountability. The city and I’m done with this. The city has committed $34 million in FY26 Executive Budget, especially designated for FIFA World Cup planning. That investment must generate measurable citywide economic returns. If structured intentionally, this tournament can strengthen neighborhood commercial corridors, bolster the hospitality industry and invested equitably in New York's creative workforce. The World Cup will come and go. What remains is the city infrastructure we build. If the city treats culture as economic development infrastructure designed, funded and governed intentionally, the benefits will extend far beyond the final match. Thank you.
Thank you.

Greetings. I’m Minky Worden and I work at Human Rights Watch, where I oversee all of our work on sport and human rights worldwide. Human Rights Watch is monitored, human rights abuses and

the run up to the Russia World Cup, to the Brazil World Cup and most recently the Guitar World Cup. We’re basically at the hundred day - oh and I should also say I’m a New York City resident and taxpayer. We’re at the 100 day countdown mark for the World Cup, which is across the U.S., Canada and Mexico and this was supposed to be both the largest World Cup in the history of the world. The First 48 Team World Cup but it’s also the first World Cup, which is governed by a human rights framework and this is a very important point. The Mayors, we applaud the Mayor’s approach that the World Cup should be joyful and vibrant and affordable but we also wanted to raise the human rights concerns around the World Cup and the World Cup is supposed to be the first that has a human rights action plan. So, now three months, 100 days before the launch of the World Cup, no one has seen the Human Rights Action Plan. Has anyone in the room seen the Human Rights Action Plan? Okay no, no one seen it. This is a - the Human Rights Action Plan was mandated for all 16 host cities by FIFA and it’s very important. So, we all saw the Acting ICE Director Alliance has said that ICE would be providing security for the World Cup and

no one should feel secure when ICE is providing security for the World Cup. There’s also no need to do it. State and local law enforcement have shown many times that they are fully capable of doing so. Human Rights Watch documented a really worrying case at MetLife Stadium in a report last December. It was a father who went with his 10 and 14 year old sons.
Time has expired.

To the World Cup and he was arrested and handed over to ICE and deported. This was at the Club World Cup last summer and this presents - and this was a New York resident. This presents a profound risk for the World Cup coming up. If the New York City area - New York, New Jersey wants to see a return on investment for this World Cup, fans have to feel safe and that means that this World Cup cannot become an ICE enforcement zone. Thank you.

Thanks for the opportunity. My name is Tarek Pertew. I represent an organization called NYC Footy, which is the largest participation soccer league in the nation. It was founded in New York where we have 60,000 New Yorkers participating, New York adults participating annually in our leagues

and I’m here just to speak uhm first just about the sport and the players. We didn’t touch too much on that reality the World Cup is that there are actual soccer fanatics that want to experience this World Cup at the height of what I call the brain, the soccer brain is going to be swelling significantly but the accessibility for participation in this sport is extremely low and I’d say stunted with antiquated policies and rules in this particular city and I want to call it a few things. I want to call it a few quick facts. One, soccer is overtaking baseball, it’s the third most popular sport in the country. Soccer has seven times the demand for field space in New York City over baseball and softball, which currently has a significant priority over soccer. 40 percent of New Yorkers are foreign born. When you factor that in with also soccer being in demand with Americans in general, this is the perfect opportunity and it’s a perfect opportunity to unite the entire city around this moment. It’s going to be the largest entertainment event in the history of the city and uhm one thing that we’ve seen is the ability to actually participate in this sport in New York. It’s difficult thinking about lighting alone.

There’s not a single lit field in New York City between Grand Street on the Lower East Side and Harlem in East Harlem. Not a single lit field. On the West side there’s only one on the Clinton Playground and soccer only gets priority considerations in the fall and winter, when there’s - uh when sun sets to 4 or 5 o’clock. So, my ask is to make park space more accessible particularly during the World Cup. Invest in temporary lighting solutions for the majority of fields where that is possible. We’ve already submitted numerous proposals to the Parks Department without response over the years.
Your time is expired.

Thank you and final point is equipment. The New York City Parks Department has just removed equipment from the majority of fields, making it to play soccer on all these large spaces almost impossible for youth and adults or community members that can’t afford to bring their own goals to and from fields. We as a lead can. It’s extremely difficult to transport goals to and from fields. We think about the community that cannot participate.

And lastly, I want to echo the previous gentleman's statement on the moratorium on permits. While we sit and wait for FIFA to tell public spaces as well as private public partnerships, like the Brooklyn Bridge Park Corporation, where we don’t even know if we’re going to have a summer league there. We have 500 players playing there every single Sunday because they have to wait to hear back from the Parks Department. So, that's holding us back as well.

Good afternoon Madam Chair. My name is Michele Dottin. I am the representative for the Independent Drivers Guild. I am also a licensed TLC driver and we are the largest driver based led advocacy organization representing over 80,000 for hire vehicle drivers in New York City and over 250,000 drivers across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Illinois and Florida founded in 2026. We are the leading driver organization in the nation. Uber and Lyft workers unite for fear of the industry. Our members will be a critical part of moving fans, visitors and workers for and from MetLife Stadium and across the region during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. They are ready to do their part. What we’re asking today is that the city do theirs. Our

concerns boil down to three practical asks. First, designated pick up and drop off staging areas, where drivers can lawfully wait for passengers without fear of being ticketed or subjected to heavy handed enforcement. If the city wants for-hire vehicles to efficiently move large numbers of people in and out of the World Cup venues, it has to create the conditions that make that possible. Second, extend bus lanes access following late matches. In Brooklyn, bus lane restrictions operate on a weekly basis, Monday through Friday 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., which can give flexibility and allow the drivers to move even faster, not you know, not have to bottleneck. We are asking the city to alleviate whether that and enforcement standard or similar flexibility can be applied in corridors serving World Cup venues after late matches to accelerate post match disbursal and reduce good luck. Third, clear advanced signage -
Your time has expired.

Throughout the event. Footprints of drivers low where FIFA zones are, which lanes are available and where they can legally wait or drop off. This is a low cost, high impact and

benefits everyone on the road. None of this is unreasonable. Designating staging, extending lane flexibility after late matches. The plain language signage, operational decisions that can and should be made before the first match kicks off. Our members will be on the road before dawn and after midnight making this event function. We are asking only that the city meet us with the same level of preparation and good faith our drivers will bring to every shift. We will also help protect and keep you know visitors safe. Those who want to take private cars, like us, Uber and Lyft.

Thank you all for your testimony and for raising very important points around the logistics of the Cup and the industry surrounding it that are going to be impacted. I want to start with the Culture and Arts policy Institute. You mentioned designated anchor organizations in each borough. Have those organizations been identified?
Uhm, I think that’s you know for the city to decide. In the past, when we had to move money really fast because we’re in March, right?
Right.

What we do - we took advantage of the partnership that the city has with CIGs that really quickly can move money outside of the city coffers. It could be a CIG in each borough, it could be designated and then that CIG could help you know the regrant money outside the other organizations.

Hmm, hmm, that makes sense. Thank you. Thank you for sharing. Uhm, and for the IDG, uhm have you identified what you expect the increase and demand will be around the cup and you know what that burden will place on your drivers?

Yeah, actually we do expect this to be high, only because we’re talking about over a million people right and even with subway, there I guess stressing high that MTA and our buses can do this job. They can’t. On a regular day, we can’t even get space on the subway platforms, the buses, they’re not going to extend that much- that many more buses right? But what we can do, we can work together to make it logistically possible, because there’s also the safety and also the trafficking issues that could happen at these events, right? So, if we have proper signage for our drivers, making sure that all the

participants and the visitors go to the correct vehicles. You know because they’ve been drinking, they’ve been doing this right, they’re having a good time and those little gaps. So, if you all can give our members something that indicates FIFA, only those cars, the riders will know to get into, we do expect on a regular day, you know we can transform about 80,000 rides in one day. So, when you add about a million visitors on top of regular public and just as Council Member Avilés said, they have issues when a normal event happens on them being able to get to work because they have not adjusted the number of riders that’s going to be added to the system. So, we do anticipate at least a million rides additional to our drivers and currently we have 85,000 licensed drivers but Uber and Lyft has another 50,000 that they can activate. So, if we have the proper, you know roadways and shared roadways, it will help everything flow better.

Thank you and I wanted to ask NYC Footy - I’m interested in the players as we talked about before and getting uhm, you know people who weren't actually able to watch the cup, participate. So, you said, the demand for soccer

relative to other sports. Is that just much higher interest or more about a lack of space for players in the city or a combination?

So, that metric is just interest alone. So, that information comes from the parks Department when they shared how many applications came through for softball and baseball in a softball, baseball priority season and soccer just blew it away and they don’t make space for soccer nearly as much in the spring and summer. We are one of the top two holders in the city and we don’t have a single renewable field for soccer in the spring or summer. It’s incredible and that’s to me, it’s just answering the needs of New Yorkers. They’re telling me they want to play soccer. It’s the most popular participation sport in this city as players, youth and adult uhm and it’s obviously going to hit a head here in the World Cup. So many New Yorkers are already playing soccer. I think they’re going to really identify more strongly with the sport because it’s going to be on home turf. This is amazing, again, the most largest entertainment event in history of this city and the city is not prepared for that at all and like folks have said, permits have

already gone out for spring and summer. It’s too late really. It’s almost too late for this city to solve for that part of it, the priority part but it’s not too late to invest in temporary lighting so that you can suddenly unlock thousands of hours at fields so that youth can extend their play and adults can come on later and participate safely under the lights. And I do want to say that on just your point real quick, I uh, went to numerous Club World Cup games, which was a little bit a teaser for this World Cup and the transportation side, it was not ready at all for what was going on there at all. Even when you got to the stadium, the confusion alone, where private cars were supposed to go, it was unbelievable. So I just want to echo your thought on that, and I do - sorry, I just want to mention one thing. Why is this important economically? Each one of these groups that comes together and participates in a lead that they can rely on every single week, that’s a big component of youth and adults recreational, mental, social and physical wellness on a weekly basis. So, they know it’s going to happen every single week. It becomes a core part of their routine, a

core part of their social lives and the economy that they generate outside of soccer is significant in this city. They might participate at the field, they go to a café before to grab their coffee. They go to a bar or restaurant later to have a meal. This- it drives so much economic activity that if you do unlock these fields through accessibility, it’s going to generate an extraordinary amount of additional income for the city and for the local businesses that surround these parks and fields.

Can I add one more thing? Our drivers are all independent contractors. They are single business owners. So, that’s also small businesses that you would be also making sure that they get a decent piece of the pie in this event as well.
Thank you all for your testimony. I really appreciate the time.
One quick thing. You know I came here thinking that Arts and Culture were the only ones left out of the planning. Well, I feel better that you know we’re not the only ones. I’m really worried.
I don’t know if I feel good about that.

THE SCALE OF THE OPPORTUNITY The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the largest sporting event on Earth—larger than the Olympics, larger than the Super Bowl. This expanded 48-team tournament will be co-hosted across the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The New York/New Jersey region has been selected to host eight matches, including the World Cup Final on July 19, 2026. The match window runs 37 days, from June 13 through July 19. These are not just games—they are global events that will bring passionate, high-spending fan bases from every continent to our city.

The FIFA World Cup is more than a sporting event. It is a catalyst to complete New York City’s post- COVID recovery. Our vision is a strategy that prioritizes public safety through presence, equity through visibility, and vibrancy through creativity—ensuring that the economic benefits of this global event reach every borough, every neighborhood, and every New Yorker, and that the investment pays dividends long beyond summer 2026. I want to be candid with this Committee about the critical challenges that threaten to undercut our city’s ability to capitalize on this moment. 1. THE LODGING CAPACITY GAP: TEMPORARILY LIFT HOME-SHARING RESTRICTIONS This is the most urgent issue I want to bring to your attention. New York City faces a serious lodging capacity gap heading into the World Cup, and our current short-term rental restrictions are making it worse. The NYC Comptroller reported hotel occupancy averaging 88 percent in October and November 2025— during a normal fall season, not a month-long global mega-event. Since Local Law 18 took effect in September 2023, active short-term rental registrations have plummeted to approximately 3,000 citywide, down from more than 38,000 active listings on a single platform in early 2023. That is a more than 90 percent reduction in available visitor lodging outside the traditional hotel market. Hotels alone cannot absorb a 37-day surge of international visitors. The families traveling from Brazil. The travel groups from Senegal and Morocco. The budget-conscious fans from across the United States. These visitors rely on short-term rentals precisely because hotels are too expensive or too small for their needs. A family of four or five cannot fit into a standard hotel room. Two couples traveling together cannot afford $500-a-night rooms for a week-long stay. The economic loss mechanism is brutally simple: a family that cannot find an affordable place to stay in Brooklyn or Queens will rent an apartment in Jersey City instead. Once outside the five boroughs, everything they spend—morning coffee, dinners, retail, local transit—goes with them. New York City ends up subsidizing the economies of its competitors during the very event it worked hard to co-host. Our preliminary analysis estimates that between 300,000 and 600,000 room-nights of demand may go unmet by current in-city hotel supply, representing between $186 million and $460 million in visitor spending that leaks to New Jersey and surrounding markets rather than remaining in the five boroughs. As such, we are asking for a narrowly tailored, 37-day temporary suspension of the short-term rental ban for the World Cup window—June 13 through July 19, 2026—to allow platforms like Airbnb and Vrbo to legally connect visitors with available apartments and rooms in the five boroughs. Thirty-seven days is too short to structurally affect the residential rental market, but it may be long enough to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in visitor spending that the city would otherwise forfeit. Other World Cup host cities are already taking action. Parkville, Missouri, voted to temporarily lift its short-term rental restrictions for the tournament. When they walk into a bar or restaurant in the East Village or Williamsburg with only their foreign driver’s license, they will be turned away—not because the bar wants to refuse them, but because the bartender has no legal protection for accepting that ID. New Jersey has already recognized and solved this problem. Governor Murphy signed the World Cup Hospitality Act, creating special event liquor licenses and modernizing hospitality rules for the tournament. Kansas City successfully passed legislation extending bar hours specifically for the World Cup. New York has done nothing equivalent for the city’s bars and nightlife—the very establishments where visitors will spend some of their most discretionary dollars. We urge this Committee to work with our state delegation to pursue a temporary amendment to ABC Law § 65-b for June and July 2026, adding valid foreign driver’s licenses and passport cards to the list of acceptable IDs for affirmative defense purposes. We also support authorizing TSA-approved digital IDs for age verification, and granting liability protection to venues using approved international ID scanner technology. These are low-risk, high-reward administrative fixes that would save our small businesses millions. On the same note, we ask the Council to consider extended alcohol service hours during the tournament. Visitors from different time zones will be seeking hospitality late into the night. Strict closing times will push commerce to unregulated alternatives. We support designating specific commercial districts as temporary 24-hour zones where noise ordinances are relaxed and late-night dining, markets, and cultural programming can capture the “City That Never Sleeps” energy that defines our global brand. Following the successful legislative model adopted by fellow host city Kansas City, New York should implement a temporary 5:00 AM liquor service extension for the 2026 World Cup to remain competitive as a global tourism destination and accommodate international viewing schedules We also support extending the Expanding overnight transit service between 2:00 and 5:00 AM during the tournament would ensure safe, reliable access for the hospitality workers who sustain this economy. 3. ENSURING A WELCOMING ENVIRONMENT FOR INTERNATIONAL VISITORS Tourism and business leaders across the region are expressing growing concern that federal immigration enforcement activity and broader geopolitical tensions could deter international visitors from coming to New York this summer. This is not abstract. International visitors spend four to five times what domestic tourists typically spend. Reports of detained tourists at U.S. borders have received significant media coverage in Europe and Latin America. A prominent European tourism official recently described the cumulative effect as a growing feeling among potential visitors that they are simply not welcome.

NYC Tourism + Conventions has launched an international advertising campaign to counter this perception, but this Council has a role to play. We urge you to make a clear, bipartisan statement that New York City welcomes every visitor to the World Cup, and to work with the administration to ensure that the visitor experience—from airport arrival to neighborhood exploration—reflects the best of what this city stands for. As part of that effort, we propose an “NYC Welcome Corps”: 500 or more temporary, uniformed Civilian Safety and Hospitality Ambassadors deployed to subways and commercial corridors, with hiring prioritized from CUNY students, NYCHA residents, and local youth. These ambassadors would provide wayfinding assistance, de-escalate friction through presence rather than force, and serve as a welcoming face for international guests and New Yorkers alike. This is a service surge, not a policing surge—and it creates jobs in the communities that need them most. 4. SMALL BUSINESS READINESS AND EQUITABLE ECONOMIC IMPACT ACROSS ALL FIVE BOROUGHS The economic benefits of the World Cup cannot be allowed to concentrate in Manhattan hotel lobbies and stadium luxury boxes. We must ensure that the rising tide lifts small businesses in every borough. We have already begun this work, and I want the Committee to know what the private sector is doing— and where we need the city’s partnership. Last year, our Chamber helped launch the Summer of Opportunity Coalition, a group of chambers, BIDs and other organizations designed to maximize the local economic impacts of 2026 summer events throughout the five boroughs. Here are some of our suggestions: Economic Visibility and Activation. The Coalition is working with Live XYZ to scale a real-time, blockby-block map of storefront businesses, public spaces, and events across all five boroughs—a dynamic guide showing visitors exactly where to watch matches, eat, shop, and experience the city. We have also created a free Summer 2026 Live NYC Map allowing any small business to get listed and drive foot traffic. We are asking the city to leverage its own marketing channels to promote this infrastructure and to invest in digital outreach teams that can reduce the digital divide by ensuring every storefront—especially in the outer boroughs—can be found online and promoted to visitors. Access to Capital. Undercapitalized small businesses may struggle to afford the upfront costs of fulfilling World Cup vendor contracts—equipment, inventory, staffing, and compliance expenses. We are asking the administration to partner with local Community Development Financial Institutions to offer affordable loan financing to help small businesses cover these costs, ensuring local vendors are operationally prepared and that major event procurement includes diverse neighborhood businesses. Street Activation. Current restrictions on street fair permits create a missed opportunity. We are asking the city to issue additional permits during summer 2026 for street festivals, block parties, farmers markets, and commercial events that would provide small businesses and vendors with low-barrier opportunities to reach visitors, generate sales, and disperse foot traffic beyond overcrowded tourist areas. Micro-Insurance for Pop-Ups. Small vendors, artists, and pop-ups cannot afford the commercial liability insurance required to rent vacant storefronts or activate public plazas. We are asking the administration to use its leverage to negotiate a bulk, group-rate short-term liability policy—allowing vendors to purchase “by-the-day” or “by-the-week” coverage at a fraction of market cost. The city acts as the broker,

not the insurer. This alone could unlock hundreds of vacant storefronts for temporary use by local entrepreneurs. Cultural Fluency. International visitors may be unfamiliar with U.S. tipping norms, unintentionally reducing earnings for our service workers. At the same time, many small businesses cannot accept international digital payment platforms like Alipay and WeChat Pay, which are commonly used by global travelers. We support a “Support Our Service Workers” tipping education campaign in all tourist materials, and a technical assistance fund to help small businesses upgrade POS systems to accept international digital wallets. FIFA Brand Rules and Small Business Protection. I also want to flag an issue that many small business owners are not yet aware of. FIFA enforces strict “Brand Exclusion Zones”—typically a twokilometer radius around stadiums and fan sites—where commercial signage, marketing language, and even promotional chalkboard specials are heavily regulated to protect official sponsors. Businesses inside these zones cannot use the words “World Cup,” “FIFA,” or “2026,” display the official logo or mascot, or create any association with non-sponsor brands. A pizzeria can welcome fans, but it cannot advertise a “World Cup Special.” Violations can result in cease-and-desist orders and fines. We need the city to issue clear, plain-language guidelines well in advance so our small businesses understand the rules and can participate in the excitement safely—without fear of aggressive enforcement. 5. GLOBAL COMPETITIVENESS: RESTORE TOURISM FUNDING Finally, I want to address an issue that extends beyond the World Cup but will determine whether we maximize its long-term benefits. NYC Tourism + Conventions is significantly underfunded compared to competitor destinations like London, Las Vegas, and Singapore, and we are losing global market share as a result. Tourism generates the tax revenue that funds housing, transit, and social services. A wellfunded tourism bureau is the only entity capable of executing the “borough dispersion strategy”— marketing Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island to visitors who would otherwise stay exclusively in Manhattan. We urge the Council to support restored and increased baseline funding for the city’s official destination marketing organization. CIVIC VIBRANCY: MAKING THE CITY WORTHY OF THE MOMENT Beyond the economic and regulatory challenges, the Summer of Opportunity Coalition has developed a set of proposals to ensure that the city itself is vibrant, welcoming, and memorable for the millions of visitors and residents who will experience it. A “Neighborhood Stage” registry would create a reservation system for musicians and performers at hightraffic public spaces—reducing turf conflicts, distributing entertainment to the outer boroughs, and ensuring artists get paid through QR-code cashless tipping. A “Good Neighbor” public service campaign through LinkNYC, subway ads, and social media would invite residents to be part of the team— combating tourist fatigue with civic pride. And “Green Guardian” youth teams stationed at fan hubs would manage waste diversion, providing fair-wage employment while solving the sanitation challenges that plague large-scale events.

These are not expensive, speculative proposals. They are practical, implementable ideas that create jobs, support artists and entrepreneurs, and make the city a better place—not just for the summer, but permanently. OUR SPECIFIC ASKS OF THE COUNCIL In summary, the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce respectfully asks this Committee and the full Council to take the following actions: 1. Enact a 37-day temporary suspension of Local Law 18’s short-term rental restrictions for the World Cup match window (June 13–July 19, 2026), allowing platforms like Airbnb and Vrbo to legally operate in the five boroughs and preventing hundreds of millions of dollars in visitor spending from leaking to neighboring markets. 2. Work with the state delegation to pass a temporary amendment to ABC Law § 65-b for June and July 2026, adding foreign driver’s licenses, passport cards, and TSA-approved digital IDs to the list of acceptable identification for alcohol service, and granting safe-harbor liability protection to venues using approved international ID scanner technology. 3. Authorize extended alcohol service hours and designate temporary 24-hour commercial zones during the tournament to capture late-night visitor spending, and work with the MTA to expand overnight transit service between 2:00 and 5:00 AM for the hospitality workforce. Extending the alcohol service hours to 5:00 AM for the duration of the World Cup will provide a critical economic boost to NYC’s hospitality industry while allowing international fans to gather and celebrate in a regulated, communal setting. 4. Issue a clear, public statement that New York City welcomes all World Cup visitors and fund an “NYC Welcome Corps” of 500+ Civilian Safety and Hospitality Ambassadors deployed to subways and commercial corridors, with hiring prioritized from CUNY students, NYCHA residents, and local youth. 5. Direct city agencies to coordinate with the Summer of Opportunity Coalition on small business readiness, including promoting the Live XYZ economic visibility platform, issuing additional street fair permits, partnering with CDFIs on affordable lending, brokering a microinsurance pool for pop-up vendors, and publishing plain-language guidance on FIFA Brand Exclusion Zone rules. 6. Restore and increase baseline funding for NYC Tourism + Conventions to ensure the city can execute a borough dispersion strategy that markets all five boroughs to international visitors and sustains the economic gains of the World Cup beyond summer 2026. CLOSING The 2026 FIFA World Cup is not just a sporting event. It is a test of whether New York City can still seize a global moment and turn it into broad-based economic opportunity for our businesses, our workers, and our communities. Every other host city in this tournament is asking itself the same question we should be asking: What do we need to do right now to make sure we don’t leave money, jobs, and momentum on the table?

For New York, the answer starts with unlocking lodging capacity, removing outdated regulatory barriers, and preparing our small businesses to compete. A temporary lift of the short-term rental ban is the single highest-impact action this Council can take before the opening whistle. It costs the city nothing, risks nothing to the long-term housing market, and stands to return hundreds of millions of dollars to the five boroughs. The foreign ID fix, the extended hours, the Welcome Corps, the street activation—these are the complementary moves that turn a good summer into a great one.
